title: Labels that matter: open-ended, benchmark, TRI, categories, index funds
objectives: Explain open-ended vs closed-ended funds and what a benchmark is.
Say why SEBI requires comparison against a TRI benchmark.
body_md:
Most equity and debt funds are open-ended: units can be bought or sold on any business day. A closed-ended fund locks money until maturity. Every fund is compared against a benchmark index; SEBI requires the comparison against the TRI (Total Return Index), which includes dividends, so the comparison is like-for-like. SEBI's standard fund categories (large cap, mid cap, flexi cap, liquid and others) let similar funds be compared, and index funds and ETFs passively copy an index, usually at lower cost.

| Term | Plain meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open-ended fund | You can buy or sell units on any business day | Most equity and debt funds |
| Closed-ended fund | Money is locked until maturity; units may trade on an exchange | Fixed maturity plans |
| Benchmark | The index a fund is compared against | Large-cap fund vs Nifty 100 |
| TRI (Total Return Index) | Benchmark version that includes dividends; SEBI requires funds to compare against TRI | Fair, like-for-like comparison |
| Fund categories | SEBI's standard labels (large cap, mid cap, flexi cap, liquid, etc.) so similar funds can be compared | Each AMC can have one fund per category (with some exceptions) |
| Index fund / ETF | A passive fund that copies an index instead of picking stocks; usually lower cost | Nifty 50 index fund |
example: A large-cap fund is compared with the Nifty 100 TRI, not with a small-cap index or with another fund's absolute return.
say: We compare this fund with its TRI benchmark, which includes dividends.
An index fund copies its index instead of picking stocks.
never: This fund beat its benchmark last year, so it will do so again.
A closed-ended fund can always be redeemed any day.

check.q: Fund A has NAV ₹10 and Fund B has NAV ₹200. Which is cheaper?
o: Neither; NAV level doesn't make a fund cheap
check.why: Neither; NAV level doesn't make a fund cheap. Returns depend on how much the NAV grows, not where it starts.
